raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular myocardial deposition of misfolded protein fibrils, most commonly immunoglobulin light chain (AL) amyloid and transthyretin amyloid (ATTR) [1,2]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma-cell disorder and is a hematologic emergency because circulating light chains are directly cardiotoxic and survival is driven by rapidity of diagnosis and clone suppression [3,4]. ATTR results from dissociation and misfolding of the transthyretin tetramer; it may be hereditary (ATTRv) or age-related wild-type (ATTRwt) [5]. Once considered rare, ATTR cardiomyopathy is increasingly recognized among older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), aortic stenosis, atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, carpal tunnel syndrome, biceps tendon rupture, and lumbar spinal stenosis [6-8].

Clinically, cardiac amyloidosis typically presents with exertional dyspnea, edema, exercise intolerance, orthostatic hypotension, atrial fibrillation, low-flow/low-gradient physiology, or progressive conduction disease. Discordance between increased ventricular wall thickness and low electrocardiographic voltage is classic but insensitive. Echocardiography often shows concentric wall thickening, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, and reduced longitudinal strain despite preserved ejection fraction; the “apical sparing” strain pattern is helpful but not definitive [9]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal myocardial nulling, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume support diagnosis and have prognostic value [10,11].

The central diagnostic task is to identify amyloid type. All suspected patients should undergo serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation to evaluate for AL amyloidosis. If a monoclonal protein is present, tissue confirmation and amyloid typing—preferably by mass spectrometry—are essential, because monoclonal gammopathy is common in older adults and can coexist with ATTR [4,12]. In the absence of a monoclonal protein, grade 2 or 3 myocardial uptake on technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy (99mTc-PYP, DPD, or HMDP), confirmed with SPECT to exclude blood-pool artifact, establishes ATTR cardiomyopathy noninvasively [13-15]. Genetic testing is required for all ATTR patients to distinguish ATTRv from ATTRwt and to guide family screening [16].

Risk stratification relies on cardiac biomarkers and functional status. In AL amyloidosis, troponin, NT-proBNP, and involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference define validated Mayo staging systems and identify patients at highest early mortality risk [17,18]. In ATTR, NT-proBNP, troponin, estimated glomerular filtration rate, six-minute walk distance, and New York Heart Association class help estimate prognosis and therapeutic benefit [19,20].

Management combines meticulous heart-failure care with amyloid-directed therapy. Loop diuretics remain the cornerstone for congestion; mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists may be useful, whereas beta-blockers, renin–angiotensin inhibitors, and vasodilators are often poorly tolerated because stroke volume is fixed and autonomic dysfunction is common [6]. Atrial fibrillation is frequent; anticoagulation is generally favored when atrial arrhythmia occurs because atrial mechanical dysfunction and thrombus risk may be disproportionate to CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. Pacemakers treat bradyarrhythmias, but the role of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators is individualized.

For AL amyloidosis, therapy must urgently suppress the plasma-cell clone. Contemporary regimens include bortezomib-based therapy and, for eligible patients, autologous stem-cell transplantation; daratumumab plus cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone has improved hematologic and organ responses in newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis [21,22]. In ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations and is most effective when started before advanced functional decline [23]. Acoramidis, another TTR stabilizer, improved hierarchical clinical outcomes in ATTR cardiomyopathy [24]. Gene-silencing therapies that reduce hepatic TTR synthesis have transformed ATTR polyneuropathy and are increasingly relevant to cardiomyopathy: patisiran preserved functional capacity in ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, while earlier patisiran and inotersen trials established the disease-modifying principle in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy [25-27]. Diflunisal and tafamidis also demonstrated TTR stabilization benefits in neuropathy populations, although tolerability and renal or gastrointestinal toxicity constrain diflunisal use [28,29]. Overall, cardiac amyloidosis has shifted from a late autopsy diagnosis to a treatable cardiomyopathy; earlier recognition, accurate typing, and timely disease-modifying therapy are now the determinants of outcome [30].
